entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part I.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: October 28, 1989 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following interview was conducted by Bob Zybach with Wanda Marcks Cook at her home in Portland, Oregon on October 28, 1989.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. German Russians

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't we start about the [water] spring and go back to your parents and what brought them to there [Soap Creek Valley].

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can tell you about the spring after we get there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I've got a note on it. Let's start with your mother's family: Where they came from, when they came to the United States and what took them to the Soap Creek Valley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't tell you what part of Germany my mother's people came from, but they moved to Wisconsin. And she was born at Sheboygan, Wisconsin, and then as a young woman she moved to South Dakota with her two brothers and they had a dairy farm about three miles from Aberdeen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know your mother's maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maurer, M-a-u-r-e-r.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And when they went to Wisconsin, do you remember about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I couldn't tell you, my mother and father [Louis Guideo Marcks] were married in 1889, Ithink.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So did they get there by the railroad? That would be about railroad.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then you told me earlier about when they were in Wisconsin, the Germans moved into the hills and they had trouble clearing timber.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it must. . if. . They had to work so much harder to clear and to be able to cultivate their farms. Cultivate the land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was a whole colony of Germans there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. There must have been quite a few.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how they cleared the farms that they dealt with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I know nothing about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so they went to South Dakota. Your mother's family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And my mother didn't know any of my father's people until after they were married. They had been married about a year and they went back to Wisconsin on a visit. And I think that's the only time that she ever met them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the old man was. . she said he had a terrible temper. And. . you know, father was the ruler in the house. And he was unreasonable.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Her father-in-law was unreasonable?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Her father-in-law, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not her husband?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then. . her husband's family was also a colony of Germans that had gone to

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wisconsin?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so. . both of your parents were.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, my father came from Berlin, however. My father, when he was six years old, came over in the steerage and as I understand it, they moved to Wisconsin too. And then it was the younger ones as they grew up that were the ones that scattered and moved farther west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that Sheboygan, also?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know your maternal grandmother's maiden name or your paternal grandmother's maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother's name was Gingerich.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Do you know how to spell that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nice German name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you spell it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. G-i-n-g-e-r-i-c-h, I would imagine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That sounds right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let me look when you get it down on paper.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Like my name, [anglicized]. NGangricht or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have a picture of my father and mother when they were married'.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's right on my. . Last on my list is photos. I was hoping you would have some photos, but we can do that maybe at the very last because what I like to do is to develop any kind of series of photos that you have that we can put with the tape so that the people know what you look like and what your parents look like, the people look like in Soap Creek Valley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When my father was six years old, he was whittling and the knife slipped and cut his eye so he was blind in one eye. It changed the color. He had brown eyes naturally but the one eye that was injured was blue. They always called him the "cross eyed Dutchman." He wasn't exactly cross eyed but that one eye was slanted just a little bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. You said he was trained to make wagons and carriages?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was only six years old when this happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. So

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But he was trained as a wagon maker, not cabinet, just a wagon maker. The wagon beds. [Perfectionist - beautiful carpentry tools, took care with them - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Perfectionist - beautiful carpentry tools, took care with them - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So then when your parents got married in 1889, that was in South Dakota?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then when did they. . When they first lived together in South Dakota did they farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. My father was a collector for the Deere Farm Equipment. . machines, Deere machines. And he drove ponies all around the country collecting from the . . what they called the SIGem Russians". Most of them were German or Russian, but they called them "German Russians." And that would be the generation before my dad. They would be older than my dad. Not necessarily a generation, but they would be older. They would be established on their farms, [Sod shanty - dirt floors - WMC]. Of course in South Dakota everything is a straight line [property lines - WMC}, they

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 1 This photograph is currently in the possession of Wanda's granddaughter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: don't meander all over like in Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. I think in Soap Creek they followed the hill sides but in South Dakota they just followed the lines. There are no hills or streams to worry about.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Speaking of that, my dad was so disgusted with the farming that had gone on at that place [Soap Creek] because if there was a hollow place where they . . roses would grow up, sweet briar, roses, they just plow around it. And of course, that area as big as this room and more would be wasted. Well, dad would fill that in and he would clear it out and clean up the fields a lot. And he improved the soil and built the fences. Fenced the whole thing. Split the oak, cut the oaks on the place and split it into fence posts. Of course they would be rotted away now [About 1906 survey - plan to sell lots, rail fences broken down - WMC].
bracketed_corrections: [About 1906 survey - plan to sell lots, rail fences broken down - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you're talking about on Soap Creek Valley, not South Dakota?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm talking about the Valley, not. yes.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. Eureka, South Dakota

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In South Dakota, he collected and then it was there where they saved their money and then moved west. And I was born the year that they extended the railroad west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Whichwas. .18..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ninety-five.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: . . 95. But that meant he came west to Eureka. In Eureka, did he work on the railroad across the United States?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he didn't work on the railroad. It was in Eureka when I was a child, that he was collector for the Deere machinery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so he started in South Dakota collecting for Deere Machinery?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then he moved out west and kept his job?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And farmed, he bought the farm and moved us onto the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In Soap Creek. Okay, so he. . in South Dakota,.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was working for a company and when he came west he worked for himself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so in Eureka, when he came out to Eureka, California, was he.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: (laughter) Not Eureka, California; Eureka. . that's what's confusing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that's where we're getting confused.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Eureka, South Dakota.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. You kept saying Eureka and I thought. . I'm a western boy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm sorry. They were married in Aberdeen and they moved to Eureka and that's where he got.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we're back to South Dakota, I thought we were off to Ca4fornia. (laughter)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never was in California, I never lived in California.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. The Marcks' Farm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, he came out to Oregon.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He came out the year ahead and scouted around looking for a place. And he found

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: this farm. Three hundred and forty-eight acres for sale.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the name of the farm, what they called it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It didn't have a name. I don't even know the name of the man they bought from. I was just a kid. Life was just a bowl of cherries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He came out a year ahead of time and found the farm, three hundred and forty-eiglu acres.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bought it and the next year moved the family out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the Glender brothers were already established?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And I think Goviers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What's happened to the Goviers?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think there's still some around. I haven't had a chance to talk to them yet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, is that so. Well, I haven't heard the name mentioned at any time in any of this talk, you know, through the years when Hilda phoned me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that would be Hilda. . Olson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hilda Olson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was Alva Govier and Elmer [Govier].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Elva and Elmer Govier?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Alva. Govier, I think, is a French name. But their mother [Sadie R. Govier2] was born on an Indian Reservation, but she was not an Indian.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She may have been a Metis; a half breed French Canadian?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was. . She never went to school very much. I've heard her say, "I was manied when I was sixteen and I knew as much then as I know now." That gives you an idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that a point ofpride? Was she proud of that or was she complaining?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bragging. My people always kind of took the attitude, "Well, it's too bad to live that long and not learn anything."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why I was asking. I'm forty-one and still learning, so f I knew eveiything by the time I was sixteen I would have had to get married too [at 16] maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm ninety-four and I'm still learning.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good, I'm trying to figure out what I'm going to be when I grow up so.. If you know everything by the time you're sixteen, that's kind of tough.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: (laughter) Let's get back to business.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay,..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where are we now. Are we still in South Dakota?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, we're out to the Soap Creek Valley on a three hundred and forty-eight acre ranch.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No fences, a tumble down house. He never even went into the house. He was interested in the land. He could see the possibilities. He put all his energies into revitalizing the soil.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 2 See monograph #09 of this series, Eugene Glender, p: 122. Her family name was slightly misspelled in the Benton County Census of 1910.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now what was his name? We haven't gotten your maiden name.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Louis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: L-e-w or L-o-u?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: L-o-u-i-s, which is a French name and then he had G-u-i-d-e-o. You pronounce it as you please. That's Italian.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Guideo.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the Marcks, M-a-r-c-k-s. That's the German spelling.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. Is that the same Marcks family that lives up by Summit? Marcks road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Same spelling, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know of any Marcks there. My family is all gone. My mother, father, and my two brothers and my sister all gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So do you have nieces and nephews from your brothers and sisters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My sister [Florence Marcks McKay] had two sons [Louis and Philip]. She was brown eyed and a very beautiful woman. Brown eyed, very dark skinned and she lived. . She married a sailor [Philip McKay Sr.], and lived in San Diego all her married life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She tanned until you would have sworn she was a Mexican.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And her children were blue eyed. I'm blue eyed and I had two brown eyed sons. Rather interesting. My father had brown eyes and my mother had blue eyes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, the way it's gone through the generations. How about your two brothers [Raymond and Wallace] did they have children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, one of them didn't have children. The older. . my older brother. . He was five years older than I. . had one son and I don't know what happened to him. He was in the service and I really don't know, there was a split up but he kept in touch with my mother for quite a while, but. . I really don't know what happened to him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, in 1904, most of the original pioneers. . just one or two, they would have been your age, but most of them had died by that point and then the land had consolidated quite often into larger farms.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I was speaking about revitalizing the soil, how he plowed just a little deeper. he never wasted a thing. All the manure went out on the land. The straw when they harvest. . when they threshed in the fall, he would have it put where it would be available to the cattle, so they could munch and protect themselves against the rain and what have you. And then after it rotted down, that was hauled out into the fields. And the Glenders had much more land and when the threshing was over, they just burned the straw and my dad would just stand there and just shake his head [in bewildered manner].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you were asking why we want to do this history, there's a good point. Right now there's a big debate on burning straw and I've talked with.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But they burned it just to get it out of the way. They burned the straw stack!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My dad let it rot down and made mulch out of it, hauled it out and put it on the land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did your dad do any burning at all, say to clear out the forest?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not one single bit of burning! Everything was . . you talk about your compost piles. That was what this straw was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Composting, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Composting, natural.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But when he opened up new fields or jf he had an oak stand that he wanted to convert to pasturage, did he cut and burn those areas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, our farm was not large enough to. The fields to cultivate here and then there was the hill with small [Douglas] fir trees that had matured since. I don't know if they've been cut now but they're ready for cutting. [Brush was burned. Logs used for fuel in fire place and kitchen range. - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Brush was burned. Logs used for fuel in fire place and kitchen range. - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did the small fir trees come in? I've been studying that pretty close. The Indians kept the hills burnt clean and then the pioneers came in and at first they grazed sheep and goats and pigs and other animals on the hill sides but when they started putting in the fences. . is that when the fir trees started growing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The fir trees were there. There was some fairly large but most of them were about oh, I would say, ten feet. I'm just guessing now. Remember I was a child.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I took everything for granted. A lot of oaks there, and my dad cut the oaks, made his own posts, split them with wedges, made his own fence posts and fenced the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Out of the oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That's the first thing. And we kept. . This was a small operation you know, but it was versatile. We kept the goats. They had a certain run. They kept the brush down on the hill. They were only kept on the hill there. They came around for salt once a week. You could tell the day that the goats would be down and then dad would go out and look them over and check them for foot trouble.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they angora?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Angoras. And the Mohair. When they sheared, it was the Mohair that paid the taxes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so what little taxes you had.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they had to. We raised everything that we ate, except the sugar and flour.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you didn't need very much money. What little money you needed was essentially for taxes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We lived high on the hog but we didn't need money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me the kind offood you ate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll tell you one that might interest you. My mother was a marvelous cook, and the Germans cooked with yeast more than they did with baking powder. And she could bake bread like nobody's business in South Dakota. When she came out here, she couldn't bake a decent loaf of bread. She worried and she stewed and she fretted. Soft wheat, you see. It didn't have the gluten in it. [Saved yeast "starter", water from boiled potatoes, "pressed" potatoes - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Saved yeast "starter", water from boiled potatoes, "pressed" potatoes - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the djfference in the wheat. So did she learn how to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So it wasn't until she got onto that. . . She had to learn all over again to handle that soft wheat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What. . were there any crops that you raised that were sold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Kept a few sheep, and there was an old. . You'll be interested in this. There was an old orchard on the place. Great big trees, over grown, mossy. And the apples were wormy. Dad kept the hogs in the orchard. When the apples fell they would run and eat it. Well, that did away with the worms. See the first apples would fall. Some very, very beautiful apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that orchard still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: An old timer, they called it a 20 ounce. It was about that big. There was a tree of 20 ounce out on this farm on Sauvies Island where they've collected cuttings. They've got a little orchard out there of all the old apple, varieties of apples. The yellow newton, the blue permaid,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those apples that you had in the orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In ours, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the blue.. 'What was the last name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Blue permaid. M-a-i-d I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your favorite apple?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Apples were just apples. We made cider by the barrel. We made our own vinegar.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You blended all the varieties. It was just more of the time that they were ripe than the variety.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a little room about that wide and long and shelves about that deep, the whole thing was [Begins gesturing with hands. See approximate measurements below] . . . and that's where they put the apples. We put newspaper down and then put the apples in there and kept them.
bracketed_corrections: [Begins gesturing with hands. See approximate measurements below]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a long narrow room with shelves with fruit on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was the fruit room. The shelves were about that deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So about..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that far apart and we just put the apples. . After we picked the apples we put them in there and kept them through the winter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the shelves would be.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the walls were insulated with saw dust. [Canned fruit, no electricity, no ice, no refrigerator - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Canned fruit, no electricity, no ice, no refrigerator - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the walls were maybe. . because this [recording] won't pick up measurements, but the walls were about 8 or 10 inches thick and the shelves were maybe twenty or twenty-four inches long and maybe ten or twelve inches deep and eight or ten inches high, something like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then the whole fruit room would process other fruits and vegetables other than apples?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Mom. . then when we got a [cream] separator - why the separator was put in there, because we could keep it clean.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many milk cows did you keep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Why. . I was the milk maid, seven or eight that I milked every morning and evening. [Turned the separator and sold cream - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Turned the separator and sold cream - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you had goats?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That wasn't in the beginning, that was when . . that was by the time I was about twelve, thirteen, fourteen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: After you've been there for four or five years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, see, I was nine . . that's right, that's right.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. The Second School

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So about 1909 or 1910? How many families were living in the Valley then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we'll start with Glenders, then Marcks, then Goviers. . Have you heard about the little house on the Marcks farm that they called "the cottage."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. I'd like to hear about it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About a mile from our house toward Goviers; Goviers is about three miles. No. About a half a mile from our house but it was on our place. Now, how that happened to be built I don't know. But there was no water in it. They had to carry the water from the creek. It was known as the cottage.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody live in it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. The school teachers lived there for a little bit rent free, you know. Dad, as I told you, dad was great for education; he would do anything to educate, you know. To improve the educational system in the Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he a member of the school board?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He made himself. I wasa kid then, I don't know about. He was a member of the school board.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right quick. And he extended the time that school was in session. [school was held four months in the fall, three months in the spring. Dad was instrumental in getting longer terms. - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [school was held four months in the fall, three months in the spring. Dad was instrumental in getting longer terms. - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And insisted on better teachers, better trained teachers and we walked the two and half miles in the mud. As I say, it never got cold enough to even freeze.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were saying the weather was dUjeren.t and Charlie Olson was saying the same thing. He thinks it's becaiLse they logged off the trees towards the top of the coast range that allowed the wind and rains to come through where there iLsed to be forests.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, a lot of difference. . We used to have a lot of fog here in Portland. Fog so thick that you'd. . Are you familiar with the city?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I lived here up until twenty years ago.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you know this Thirty-ninth and Glisan where the statue of Joan of Arc is. You could just drive around that thing and go back where you started the fog was so thick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a daily thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think the weather now is a little bit colder but clearer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's colder and far more wind, far more wind.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why do you think that happened? Do you think it's jzst one of those natural cycles where.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know. We get a lot more wind from the Columbia Gorge than we used to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And of course, now when I first came to Portland, Powell Boulevard, they were cutting the first growth firs along Powell. Out here between here and Gresham, Boring, Troutdale, and Estacada.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that was still being logged off at that time? I've got maps of Portland from 1851 where there was forest fires within our city limits now. This area here had forest fires. On Soap Creek, were they doing any logging there at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they had been logging earlier. There was a skid road right close to the school house (Soap Creek).

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the school hoiLse..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do you know about that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There 's. . I know it became a tram road in the 1930's where the school house is now. Is that the same location?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so you went to the older school. The one they call the Second School.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The old school. The one that's still there and they've painted it red now. It was painted white.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one that's there now wasn't built until 1932, it replaced an older school.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I thought when they built the. . When they no longer used the one that I went to, that's still standing there, but they weren't using it. When they enlarged the district or built a new building they built nearer the mouth of the valley. Down near Glenders. Isn't the school down near Glenders?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, they built.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no school there. There was just that old Tampico Tavern ["Arcade Saloon" in Glender] falling apart.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the only building left from Tampico that you can remember, the old Tavern?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That and Glender's house, and another house. . Beales, I think their name was Beales.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: B-e-a-l-e-s?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't thought about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now at that time the old tavern, was that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That little brat that I had to pick up and look after.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was a Beales, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Edna.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we didn't get that recorded [stoly about having to take Edna Beales to school each day]. You were talking about walking two and a half miles to school, but then after.
bracketed_corrections: [stoly about having to take Edna Beales to school each day]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was up the valley until I passed state eighth grade exams.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you went to high school in Wells.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I went to high school in Wells.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you got there by horseback?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Horseback, yes. Well, I was going to say, then when dad got so that we had. really had school in this old building up the valley, they built a shed to shelter the horses and we rode and the teacher rode horseback.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the teacher's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The teacher's name was Blake, Mrs. [Lottie] Blake. I don't remember her given name. They didn't use given names in those days. It was Mrs. Blake.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the Olsons would have been going to school and also the Moores. The Sam Moore family. Did you know the Moores? They were there right about the turn of the centuiy. They were up near Sulphur Springs, near the Olsons and then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Cooks were the nearest and then we called our the place the Sulphur Springs Stock Farm. [The Browns, Smiths, Dorgans, Moore on the hill. - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [The Browns, Smiths, Dorgans, Moore on the hill. - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's after you got married?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: After I got married.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a name for your follcs' place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the Marcks Farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just the Marcks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now on the. . I want to get the names of the hills, but when your folks had it there,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: how long did they stay?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your parents, how long did they keep that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father died. He had cancer of the liver and he died a year or two after. . let's see. . . My son's. . my son wasn't even a year old, Roy wasn't even a year old when my father died. Then mother carried on the best she could and then she sold the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who did she sell it to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Is your machine on?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you want me to tunz it off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Turn it off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. [Tells story that she doesn't want recorded].
bracketed_corrections: [Tells story that she doesn't want recorded]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's why I don't know what happened.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. Wildlife

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now your mother then where did she move after she sold the place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She moved to Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And lived here for quite awhile?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, she lived here from then on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she remarry?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She lived with me for awhile after I was on my own.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she remariy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, why did she come to Portland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where were we?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you were saying you were the last of your family 's line, but your mother sold the place and moved..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother moved to Portland and she got work here and there, as long as she could work and then when she couldn't work any more, why then we took over. We helped out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, your children, you still have your children and a couple nieces and nephews so there are.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You're talking too fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I'll slow down.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm sorry.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When. . let's go back to the farm, when your father was farming, did you ever do any fishing or did he do any hunting or did the neighbors fish and hunt there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father was a great hunter on the prairie. Prairie chickens, ducks, geese, and I can remember them driving [no cars, ponies - WMC] out in the fields, you know, and there'd be a picnic lunch and they'd [one party of five or six hunters - WMC] go hunting and the women would stay around the hay stack or wherever they managed, you know. And I used to have pictures of. . we'd. pictures of the geese and chickens and so on. But anyway when he came west and he bought a very beautiful rifle, he was going to. . do some hunting, you know, get a deer. Well, then the farm took so much of his time he never did get to go hunting, but one morning he got
bracketed_corrections: [one party of five or six hunters - WMC]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: up early and saw a deer meandering right down by the creek and he went to the house and got the gun and stopped this thing and he got such a dose of fever that he couldn't hold his gun steady and he laughed at himself after he told it. He wouldn't. probably. . It was such a beautiful animal he just wound up. he just didn't have the heart to kill it. I think that's what happened, but he said he had buck fever. That's what they called it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, they still do. So did. (end of side 1) [&plaining history project details to Mrs. Cook: "I'm trying to determine ecological changes associated with] domestic animals and how we went from wolves and bears and deer and elk in the Willamette Valley to cows and horses, and. . did you raise hogs?
bracketed_corrections: [&plaining history project details to Mrs. Cook: "I'm trying to determine ecological changes associated with]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is this on?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, it's just now starting.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I remember the coyotes. You see I was a lonely child. There was nobody to phy with. People named Smith lived next to Goviers. You were asking me what. there's a beautiful cherry orchard there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that still there? Do you know f the cherry orchard is still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Did you raise, on your farm where there was an orchard and you put the hogs in there, they had hogs, goats, some sheep, milk cows, did you raise any steers for beef?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. All milk cows, all milk cows, yes. But my dad was very fond of horses and he bought mares and bred them to very fine stallions and he raised really, very fine work horses. [He sold some, but kept a buggy horse - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [He sold some, but kept a buggy horse - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have riding horses or trade horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we had one Indian pony. He was a dear. He was a sweetheart.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say Indian pony is.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He wasn't a true pinto. He's what they call a strawberry roan.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. So..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I don't have a picture of it and I wish I did, because . . I gave that to my sister and they are with my nephew now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, on Soap Creek, did that have fish in it or beaver in it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No beaver.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Trout. Not very large, but the stream is very cold, but even as far down, we were three or four miles . . We were at least four miles from the Sulphur Springs but you could still taste the Sulphur in the creek water. And we found arrowheads on our farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was going to be my next question. Where your farm is, is now a registered Kalapuyan site, part of it. Now you found. . did you find any grinding bowls or. just arrowheads.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just arrowheads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they the little kind offinely shaped.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the biggest one we found was about like that and was white. (all well shaped)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About an inch and a half and was white. So it was agate and not obsidian.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And in perfect condition.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That could have been a fairly old one, that large and it wasn't obsidian.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Yes, it would have been. I don't know what happened to those things, I suppose my brother got them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. When you moved out west, you said the first Japanese person you ever saw was as you first moved here they were working in a cherry orchard in Portland. The farm you were living on was settled by a Black lady [Lettia Carson] and there was also near Wells, a Black man [Lew Sozahworth] that lived there in the 1870's a couple of the very few Blacks in the Pacific Northwest. Were there any Blacks that you can recall in the community or travelled through.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: None whatsoever.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. Lewis and Clark Exposition

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the first person you saw that was Black?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. It might have been when we came to the fair, Lewis and Clark Fair in 1905.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You came to that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're working on the bicentennial.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, other people that we saw. . We had relatives there in Portland so we came up a few days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Can you remember the fair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. That was the first time I tasted a Coca Cola.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At the fair.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They still had cocaine in it in those days.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My uncle bought it. Mine was a real cocaine, you betcha. I didn't like it. Stupid me. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just ahead of your time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother's brother was not married at that time. And he was awfully good to us kids, you know. He was. . we hung around him and he was conductor on the street car.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here in Portland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here in Portland, and his favorite run was to the Heights. Portland Heights.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember most about the fair? Buying your first coke must have been part of it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: one of your strong memories. Well, Uncle bought me that coke, and I remember the Forestry Building. One reason I remember the Forestry Building because after I moved to Portland until it burned down, I bet you there wasn't a year that I didn't go up there two or three times because those huge trees just, you know, those huge logs they were. . I like wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Forestry Building was important to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Forestry Building was important to me. This came from New Zealand, [shows a piece of woodwork]. Look at the workmanship on that. Roy brought me that last year when he came home from New Zealand.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: My partner [Michael Grice], who's Black [African American], is announced a project to rebuild the Forestry Building for the Bicentennial of Lewis and Clark. He's going to find this fascinating for that reason. That's a beautiful. . I guess it wouldn't be an ashtray, you

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: wouldn't.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Isn't that a beautiful piece of work?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes it is.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I like wood, I just like the feel of it. It has life. Plastic has no life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've worked with trees and wood all my l(fe and that's kind of my prejudice too. So.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where are we? We're still on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We took a visit from the farm to the Lewis and Clark Exposition.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that was just a visit, a few days visit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it's interesting to me that the Forestiy Building made such an impression on you that you went back year after year. Do you remember a slice in the Forestiy Building [exhibit of tree rings] taken from Table Mountain [Lincoln County, Oregon] that showed different dates and it had a metal cut. . I've been tiying to track that down for awhile. It was taken from Table Mountain where maybe there'd been metal there in the 1700's. Do you remember any particular exhibit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I just felt like a big piece of me went up in flames when that building burned.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Old logging equipment, wheels, steam engine, narrow gauge - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Old logging equipment, wheels, steam engine, narrow gauge - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any particular exhibit or was it actually the construction of the building itself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Construction of the building and the fact that they had the imagination to put a building like that together. The pillars, you know, were just tree trunks, huge tree trunks with the bark on them, interesting. Now, when I could stifi scramble around, it's very difficult for me to walk now, but when I go up to OMSI (Oregon Museum of Science and Industry) I go up to the . . [long pause]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Forestry Center?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Forestry Center.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was just there two weeks ago for their cultural resources [exhibit] so. . sounds like.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll be going again, I think maybe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm loolcing forward to. . . when I get a little bit further on this project of maybe going with you on a trip to Soap Creek Valley and that might be a stop. It's. . a lot of these places you're talking about are the names of the hills and it would be a lot easier jf you're there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 7. Back on the Farm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, back on the farm then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So, we're back on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we've got trout in the creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's a wonderful spring on that farm. Cold, cold, cold. And there was an old shack, we called it the spring house and the spring would overflow and under a wooden platform and that's where we kept our milk. Great big tin pans of milk about that deep, you know. And kept it cool and it would sour, naturally sour, you know. It's better than any ice cream, that sour. . that sour milk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was like a treat to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's clambered, you know. [Because it was raw milk - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Chilled clambered milk was kind of a dessert?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, or you know, snacks with sugar and cinnamon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you make your own cheese?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We made all our own butter. (cottage cheese, trick is working butter in wooden bowl with wooden paddles) Well, anyway there was a tin dipper hanging on that spring house and people would go by. Everybody in the neighborhood knew about that spring and they would stop the team, run up there and get a drink of water on the run. Nothing (unintelligible), right across. . . Some of them were strangers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that spring still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. I tried to find out and I couldn't find out too much about it. [Subsequent trip with son, Roy, failed to locate the spring.]
bracketed_corrections: [Subsequent trip with son, Roy, failed to locate the spring.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it called the Marcks Spring?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They didn't have any name. It was right close to the building, right close to the house and my dad built a. . There was a stream running through and he built a bridge across that so we could go from the house straight across and dip our water out of the spring. That's how we got our water.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the house is still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The house is still there, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did your dad build that. . that house, did your dad build that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I was going to tell you about when he saw the farm he bought the farm. He never even went into the house and when we came west and of course, there were no autos then. He took mother out to see the farm. She had never seen it and I remember seeing tears in her eyes because that house was such a tumble down thing and there was no heat. No heat in it except from the kitchen stove and this huge fireplace. It would take a back log of that big of oak, that long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the back log so it was built like this,, see, and the back log would be in there, and we built it, and that was what heated the living room, and the house and the kitchen stove. [The fireplace was huge and so the back log was huge, the fire was built in front of the back log. The fire would be banked with ashes at bedtime. The back log would be one great live coal in the morning. Coals were then taken in shovel to kitchen range to start fire there. Wonderful draft, brick hearth, broken. - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [The fireplace was huge and so the back log was huge, the fire was built in front of the back log. The fire would be banked with ashes at bedtime. The back log would be one great live coal in the morning. Coals were then taken in shovel to kitchen range to start fire there. Wonderful draft, brick hearth, broken. - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be. . The back log would be about two foot by a diameter of, maybe, afoot in diameter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, more than that. That big around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eighteen or twenty inches in diameter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And about four feet long. So the front of the fireplace, you see, was a lot like that. And nothing but just plain ordinary brick and they were pretty well broken for the hearth. And mother was very disappointed in the house. But she got busy with paint and what have you and cleaned it up [Mother was a very good seamstress, we made almost all our dresses and underwear, flour sacks. Mother kept geese down and striplet feathers, sold pillows - WMC] . . but dad never even looked at the house, he looked at the farm, see? And he built it up, fenced it, put up two big barns, built up his horses and cattle, what have you, the whole thing, and then he got sick and died. So we never got. . The house was the next thing in his plans.
bracketed_corrections: [Mother was a very good seamstress, we made almost all our dresses and underwear, flour sacks. Mother kept geese down and striplet feathers, sold pillows - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And my dad had very progressive ideas. He would have put in a house that really was a house and had planned to utilize this spring either with a pump or something, I don't know how . . I don't know what the idea was, but anyway, that would be our

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: source of water. He was a'ways very careful not to cut any of the trees around there, you see that little mound covered with tiny trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the small trees were growing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And was the source of. . held the water, you see, the spring. . for the spring. That spring welled up until the water was about that deep (5 feet). We had to dip it out, carry it to the house, heat it in a reservoir on the back of the stove.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you had fencing, different kinds of stock, trout in the creek, vely few deer, but you had coyotes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to carry on conversations with the coyotes. You know, a kid alone. They get so they can mimic the wild animals and birds. The same way with the crows, china pheasants, and jays. (My younger brother and sister were 15 months apart. Boy, when I was 8, my charges as mother was very busy. They roamed the farm like gypsies)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there a lot of crows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. We had pet crows, but strangely enough every once in a while one would disappear. I know now what happened to. . You know, crows are a nuisance. Steal! They're lots of fun, but they're as smart as whips. My dad would do away with one at a time, you see, while we were at school. We were too stupid to know it. We'd mourn them. Another crow gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He would be surreptitious about it, just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, never dawned on us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Were there other types of birds? Were there migrations of geese or ducks that you can recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they'd fly over but they. . No, there was no flatland, nothing for them to feed in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about raccoons and possums or bobcats?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, raccoons galore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about. . would you have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No possums.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were imported.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But beautiful, these beautiful silver-grey squirrels. And . . [pauses as if she is not sure what she says next should be recorded].
bracketed_corrections: [pauses as if she is not sure what she says next should be recorded]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's all right, even after we print this up, jf you see something that you don't want to say then we'll just. . strike that out. We don 't want.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm just on a little sideline, you know, the lonely kid. I got to be a pretty good marksman. We had lots of greydiggers, we called them greydiggers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still do.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I got to be a pretty good marksman with the twenty-two special, but I never went hunting for deer. They were too beautiful.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about pheasant. They were introducing pheasant in Oregon then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there were quite a few pheasants around, and I got so I talked to them, too, and they'd answer me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there problems. . did you raise chickens?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there problems with bobcats ever, or. .?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not bobcats, the skunks. Just the skunks, and the little civet cats, they'd come right around our feet and we'd stand on the porch and with a lamp in our hands, you

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: know, and they'd come sniff around, you know. Of course, you stand real still until they leave. But they're beautiful, they're far more interesting than the big skunks, but then we had both.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You. . I think I'm getting a pretty-clear picture . . you can see what I'm trying to do is pus the animals and the plants. . Now, what kind of crops did you raise?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oats. (wheat, vetch, horse feed, no barley or rye)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many acres?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't tell you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That whole lower valley was all in. was all cultivated.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there would be oats.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And my dad enlarged. Every year he'd enlarge the fields.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you had a large garden of different vegetables for your family use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had just a garden. It was fertilized from the barnyard fertilizer and we never had any irrigation whatsoever. We kept it moist by a dust mulch, hoe it every so often to keep the dust, there'd be moisture underneath. Wonderful vegetables, flavor beyond compares. . because it wasn't watered down, see, it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you grow any vegetables that would be unusual by today's standards or were they just the standard potatoes and carrots?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the standards (cauliflower, turnip, beets, onions, pie cherries), just the standard. Then mother had a little herb garden, we had raspberries. . strawberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of herbs would she grow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I beg your pardon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of herbs would she grow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Herbs?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was just a kid, I can't tell you. There was dill, catnip, she always had shallots, and what are these onions . . the Chinese, these great big

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. . not leeks..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Leeks!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She raised leeks then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but these were smaller than we see in the market now, she called them winter or bunch onions.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Then you had raspberries for your own use or for conunercial?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no. No, we didn't sell anything of that sort. That was just for the family and the house was surrounded by blue Damson plum trees, and the blue jay would come in there and. . Blue jays are interesting birds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I used to have one of those as a pet rather than crows.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They're such mimics you know. They quack like the ducks and talk like the turkeys and. . They're very interesting. And when the Damson plums were ripe, why the trees were just covered with these blue jays, these beautiful stellar jays. But we didn't have the Western jays there, like we have here in town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the stellar jays?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Just the dark blue.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever notice owls or hawks or eagles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, owls and hawks. No eagles. But I can remember walking through the woods and hearing a "whissssss" . . the owl flying by, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about cougars or bears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, it sounds like things were pretty well being farmed but the soils were depleted. You were saying, I don 't know tf we got that on the recording. But the early farmers from the South had not plowed very deep and so the top layers of the soils had been depleted through cultivation.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that was true of that grey clay farm off towards Albany where Adair. . Camp Adair was. It was the same proposition there. I don't know if anybody ever built that up.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 8. Married Life

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's records from the 1880's saying the soil was depleted then, so by 1904 that certainly had to be the case. Then you got married. Was your husband [Ernest Cook] from a family from the Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he was. . I think originally from Missouri. I think he was born in Missouri. And his father had an accident and so he wasn't able to do the hard work so he went into the feed business and he was really quite wealthy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: His father?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: His father, yes. And then they moved west because his father [grandfather] had a breathing problem and they wanted to get away from the severe winters, they moved west and they lived here in Portland. They tried California, but it was too dusty and dry. So they lived here in Portland and then the son went to Oregon State [College].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so he went to Oregon State College?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. But he was not cut out to be a farmer. Not the proper temperament.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he graduate from school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you meet him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When he bought the farm. . they bought. . His uncle [John W. Cook] bought this farm and he moved out there. [Hired man and wife in new house - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Hired man and wife in new house - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Isee.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But his father [Tyrone P. Cook] and sister [Mary L. Cook] never did move out there. Then they brought his grandmother3 from Missouri so she could live with them. They brought her out and she lived in the home here in Portland, right down here on 21st and Weidler.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now on your husband's end. . had he already graduated from college when you met him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. [His father gave him the farm - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [His father gave him the farm - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, he was out working on his uncle's farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was living on the place, that's when I met him. [His father's farm which had been purchased for him - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [His father's farm which had been purchased for him - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. So how old were you at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You would bring that up. Eighteen. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: According to Roy Cook, she was Tyrone P. Cook's mother-in-law, Elizabeth Schultz (1836-1935).

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he was maybe twenty-five?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Twenty-two.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 7venzy-two, huh. So, then when you married him, you moved on, essentially, to the Sulphur Springs Stock Farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then was that. that would have been right next to the Olson's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Olsons lived way back in the hills. Two and a half miles, way up in the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: O/z, I see. Do you know who the Cooks bought their fann from? Could they have bought that from the Moores?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. [Possibly - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. How big was it. . that farm (the Olson's)?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. It was mostly like this. they had one horse, "Yim," Jim, "Yim," and the old man worked it. The whole family, Mr. and Mrs. Olson, Charlie, and Hilda would load up the wagon with one horse and drive all these miles out (to the hop fields near Independence for weeks) and then they camped down there and on the way home they couldn't make in one day, so as they went through they'd spend the night with us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that would be the Olsons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Olsons.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Olsons would go to Suver to get their tax money for their place instead of Angoras and they'd pick hops there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the hops had to be used for brewing, so this is before prohibition?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Independence was the really. . in fact, we still raise a lot of hops in Oregon, but Independence was the huge, huge field of hops and then the dryers. [At that time Independence was said to be the hop center in the state - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [At that time Independence was said to be the hop center in the state - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any Indians used to work in those hop fields? Would any Indians come through the Soap Creek Valley that you can recall? Did you ever see Indians?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. You see that road, the road over the hill was not developed. It was just more of a wagon track.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The road from Kings Valley. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the road over the hill from Sulphur Springs to Corvallis [Mountain View - WMC]. There never was a road directly from Kings Valley into the Soap Creek Valley, and from Sulphur Springs up over the hill to Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To Lewisburg..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was nothing more than a wagon track.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so there was no road between.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: unimproved, unimproved.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was no road to Kings Valley when you were little?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No! [A little exasperated at persistence of questioning or density of questioner.]
bracketed_corrections: [A little exasperated at persistence of questioning or density of questioner.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the road [over the hill] to Lewisburg hadn't been. . it wasn't suitable for carriages?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we used to ride over it, but you couldn't. . no, you couldn't take a.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not wheeled vehicles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. [With difficulty]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that area there was that pretty open or was it densely forested?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Forested.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Large trees or small trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly alders along in there. [Along the creek, evergreens on the hills - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [Along the creek, evergreens on the hills - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Alder, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then the goat weed took over the pasture land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Goat weed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goat weed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: TWzat was the reason it took over the pasture land, why weren't the pastures maintained?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, because they're hills. How are you going to maintain a pasture on a hill like that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it spreads from the root, if you cultivate that just once you could kill it out, but you had to keep it cultivated, not only propagates from the root but from the seed, both.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the goat weed started taking over the hills and I'm assuming the trees came in, alder you say, came in. [scrub oak]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The alders were along the creek, I'm talking about right around the springs, Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, do you remember any building around Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I remember that they had a. . it was. . They had a cement wall, like a little well, you know, where it bubbled up. And people used to go up there to camp. And I'm trying to think of what the names of people that had it. That owned that. I can't remember the name. [Baker]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Charlie Olson said that there was used be a concrete fountain there at the springs and people used to come there by. . first by bicycles and then horses and then cars, that it was always a popular recreation spot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he also said there used to be a hotel there for. . but he said there was a hotel there and people just lived in it like a house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No hotel, no building there whatever. [Not in my time - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anywhere around Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No building whatever, they came in tents, lived in tents.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they go hunting from their camping spots?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just recreation, just vacation.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just to hang out with the family in a tent?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd probably fish the creek some and play around that way, hike around, but no, there was no organized play, golf or tennis, or anything. Not a thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No ball field,s?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nothing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not even a place cleared big enough for a ball field. It was right in among the alder trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And a lot of people came though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I wouldn't say lots but they'd come and go, come and go. Maybe two families that'd get together and go up and camp for a week.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they go hunting maybe back in the woods?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, nothing to hunt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you moved then to. . let's see you called it the Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Stock Farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Stock Farm. . Do you recall how big that was. . your stock farm. . how many acres?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Eleven hundred and thirty-eight4.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, eleven hundred thirty-eight acres, that's large.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but a lot of it was waste, pasture, goat weed, brush.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now was that the way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He didn't have as much cultivated land as my father's small farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. On the eleven hundred acres was that the total amount purchased by the uncle then, originally?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My husband's uncle [John W. Cook]. Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then your husband bought it from him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the uncle bought it. He was looking for a farm, John Cook was. . Ty (for Tyrone) Cook's brother and that was my husband's Uncle John and Uncle John was looking for a farm and instead of looking around and then giving them a chance to look it over, he just bought the thing. Which he was not authorized to do, but my husband's lather went along with it and stocked it and. . put my husband on the farm. But he was not cut out to be a farmer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you live there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Six years I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the time you were eighteen until you were about twenty-four you lived on. . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of livestock did ytu have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beef. . but not beef as you see it now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wizat was the d?(ference?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it wasn't the high grade that. . It was common stock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember how many head you had?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you planted an orchard at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And was that all apples?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you think that orchard is still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They cleared it by dynamiting the trees so as to get the roots out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you burn the roots up then? Did you have clearing fires?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they did with them. I suppose we burned them. What else would you do with them?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tiying to find out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We cleared the land. We probably used the trees for firewood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the trees you cleared would those have been scattered large oak? (not ve,y large)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just this little knoll, just the three acres little knoll that we planted to orchard. [We

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: " Wanda's son, Roy Cook, later said that the size of the stock farm was 1348 acres. The historical documents iii Appendix A substantiate Roy's number.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: had Percheron horses, silo for corn, planted buck wheat for my bees in the orchard - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was there ten years ago, there's a lot of little houses have been built in there, now whether they are renters or whether they bought small tracts and built those houses, people that were living there or not, I don't know. But the road. . the Soap Creek Road was just barely graded when we moved there and they kept improving it, of course, as they went along. If they were going to telephone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when cars first came into that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that about maybe 1915 or something like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wouldn't know the year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right before World War I?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But this, I just remember that a man named Smith came out and rented this place that had the nice cherry orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then he would have rented from Goviers or. . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know who owned it. (Browns?)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the house you lived in on the Sulphur Springs Stock Farm, did you build that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was built before I was married, I didn't have anything to do with that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So,..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no house on the place when they bought it. (end of tape.)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We are going to have to repeat one part of it about when you. . you moved in with your husband when you were eighteen on Sulphur Springs Stock Far,n. Tell me what your jobs were out at the farm and. . Do you. . mind going through that a third time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You want me to go through that again?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Then hopefully that will be all.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. The home is kind of the hub, and the wife is busy in the garden, child to be taken care of. Wife always takes care of the chickens, and cooks for the hands. [clean lanterns and lamps, kerosene -WMCJ

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those [hired hands] year round or seasonal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they year round?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had one the year round and during the busy season they had another one, so that made three. All those places on Soap Creek were too small, they . . harvesting was done with a binder and then doing the shock (shocking bundles). I put up a darn good shock myself. And we were speaking of the weather, on a hot afternoon you would be shocking grain and you'd look out and leaves on the trees would begin to rustle. You could depend on the sea breeze at 3:30. You could practically set your clock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Every afternoon about 3.30?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Every afternoon that cool breeze would come through, which is rather interesting, right in the foothills where.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it came from the west? If it was what we called the sea breeze it would be coming over the hills.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a sea breeze that it came from the west. You could always depend on it you know, you'd be tired and think "oh, boy, time for the sea breeze." You know what

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that would be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you then when your-first child was born?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Twenty. I was twenty the 26th of March and he was born the 6th of April.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: My wife's birthday is April 6th.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, is that so. That's Roy's birthday, and my second son [Richard E. Cook (1920- 1987)] was born four years later. I was twenty-five when my second child was born, he was born the 21st of April.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the second was born in Portland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The house that you kept house in, is that still there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it's still there and I have a picture of it [See Appendix A photograph #25 and 26,pp:79]. My granddaughter took a picture of it and I have it around somewhere else, I'll look it up and have it when you come again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But it doesn't look a bit like it did when we had it. We had it fenced in which is. most of them didn't take care of their yards. And we had water, I could water it and I had a green lawn, and it was really quite a pretty place. Small white house and you came around the curve and there was a white house and a flag and a green lawn and flowers and that's about it. (unusual -- green lawn that I mowed)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you raise flowers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Daffodils or lilacs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Daffodils, lilacs, camelliis, and roses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Raised roses, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beautiful roses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the varieties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember a beautiful red rose at the back gate. My hair was long at that time and kind of a red brown.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Auburn? (no)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I'd often pick a rose and put it in my hair, and when I took my hair down at night it would be scented by the rose, rose fragrance. My husband's grandmother [Elizabeth Schultz (1836-1935)], was fifteen years old during the Civil War and she used to tell me stories about that. She liked to come out to the farm. She was a farmer's wife and when she could come out here to visit us on the farm she was in a glory, you know, when she came out to stay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody write down in of those stories, or do you remember any of the stories?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, she told about hiding under a bridge and the soldiers came and drove away a lot of the horses and she was hiding under the bridge and she could heard the clatter of the horses, that was one thing she told me. And then, of course, the men were gone to war, and the women had to do the work in the farm. I don't know how large a farm they had, but. . she said, "Oh, it was terrible in those days for them to be tanned" and she would cover her face with a paste made out of flour and water, so that she wouldn't tan and bum.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Like they use sun screen now, as that time tan wasn't a good thing so they had to work on the farm and still keep their complexion.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Tried to. She was a very little woman and she was known as Aunt Bet [Elizabeth] in their county. She went around nursing, you know, more or less the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: new born, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who did the midwifing in. . who was your midwife?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, my son was born. . the doctor came out to the house, doctor and his wife came out for the delivery and after that we managed there was a phone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The doctor came out from Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Came out from Corvallis. He was young in Corvallis, his name was ["Doc"] Anderson. He's probably retired now, but he built up a good practice there. He was modern, naturally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you were first getting married, they were just putting in roads, they were just putting in telephones [when I was 11 or 12 - WMC], so really the lfes1yle was kind of changing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the road was there but it wasn't improved. But the telephone came and it brought a lot of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would be when I was about eleven, I would say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that pretty big news at that time. . was that a major event. . getting the telephone in?

entries.speaker: A
