entries.text: Well, yes. It was a link, link with your neighbors. Party line, everybody was on the line. And if you were smart, you wanted to be careful what you said, because you knew your neighbors were listening in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you got a phone out at Soap Creek it was pretty early, one of the first phone lines to it. Was the railroad that went through Wells was that a major link in transportation or communication at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes, with Portland and you know, that was when they had the big electric cars.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They ran electric cars all the way down into Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Portland to Eugene.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, were those real regular and dependable?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. We'd drive down [horse and buggy - WMC] to the railroad and pick up. our people and go back home and when they left we'd take them down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you went to the Lewis and Clark &position, then you went to railroad car?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did that take, do you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but they didn't have the red cars then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the red cars came later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The red cars came later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was kind of a special tourist type thing, the red cars?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. [No, they carried passengers, mail, freight express - WMC]
bracketed_corrections: [No, they carried passengers, mail, freight express - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then on the hill side up on the Stock Farm, you weren 't using those because the stock was there and there were trees growing there, alder along the creek, do you remember what was growing up along the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Scrub oak, and fir, no pine, and no spruce.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come you know your trees so well?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've always been interested in trees and woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There were native stands ofpine in that area [Kings Valley: White pine; Corvallis: Ponderosa pine] in the 1850's, do you ever remember seeing any pine?
bracketed_corrections: [Kings Valley: White pine; Corvallis: Ponderosa pine]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think there was a single pine tree on our place, and I've covered it. . pretty well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And there's no hemlock or no spruce?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No spruce, no pine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Red cedar or maple?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maple, galore. Maple and what we called a white oak, but I don't know the. . big leaf. And we were talking about the roads, right in the middle of the road, there was a great big witness tree, a great big oak. And at that time they were surveying and improving and changing the lines. We surveyed and they would cut out a great gash like this in the oak tree and here you could see the surveyors marks in the sapwood, very interesting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's still some of those standing. Some of those old witness oak, but they were large oak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The road went around this darn tree, but they took that tree out in time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the Stock Farm did you also raise any sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any goais? (no)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't too successful (sheep), I don't know whether their feed were not balanced right, we planted kale. And- that was another thing a house wife did, she went out into the fields and helped with new born lambs. Do you know anything about lambing sheep?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just enough to know i'll never do it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they came early in spring, you know, and lots of times there would be hail, very cold rain and hail mixed with it, and the little lambs get good feed, their belly full, and dried off, they can stand any amount of cold, but when they are newborn why many of time, I've slugged through the mud in rubber boots with a lamb under each arm, coaxing the ewe along to get her in the barn and bed them over night. Then I'd have to see that the lamb nursed and after that they were on their own. The next morning, turn them out and the lamb would do all right. But that was a small operation, that wasn't a big sheep ranch, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have angora goais?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not on our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, your father died right after you left home, two or three years..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then. . when your mother moved to Portland after that you were pretty much the only member of your family

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I moved to Portland before my mother did. . mother sold the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 see, so she stayed there for several years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She stayed there for quite a while, she tried. . I told you. . she tried to run it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: TWzai happened to your place, the Cooks then sell all your place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, I can't say, I don't know just when the Cooks. . (yes)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now World War 1, that would have been.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We were still on the farm, raised navy beans that year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that have any impact on your economy or your neighbors, was there anything about World War I or that was occurring that had any impact on the Soap Creek Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It changed some of the crops. . as I said, we raised beans, trying to get something that was . . would go along with the. . get a cash crop. (field corn for silage)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the beans then you were raising for military use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: White beans, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that work?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, for a few years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, on the beans, do you remember about how many acres you put in of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you still raising oats that far back in the Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Oats for hay. Oats and vetch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I'd like to get a clear idea. . what I'm tiying to do is make sure I get a clear idea of this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well, and then on the Cook farm, they would plow down by the creek and raise field corn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For the stock?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For the stock to eat in the wintertime. That's another job I had, to tramp down the sows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. Mat jobs didn't you have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well. . [motion with hands to turn off machine]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you want me to turn it off[turn off machine to give details]? I'll ask you questions and I'll get somebody to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sound's to me like you're pretty much an early day feminist. You really wanted to take your lfe in your own hands and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You're talldng too fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds to me like your were. . for that day and age and for a woman you were.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wanted to make a g of it. I had the energy and the knowledge. I had the ffl, but it takes.

entries.text: Two to tango?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was going to say that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just nying to interpret your hand 5/gnal for the recording.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It just wouldn't work out. It wasn't in the cards. Everybody isn't a farmer, you know, they may think they are, but they aren't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you sony to give up your.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It takes

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: .fannljft?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was, but it wouldn't go so the thing to do is do the best you can with what you have to work with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So then..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That sounds a little callous but I don't. . I was too young to understand.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds pretty practical.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, after all you don't live another forty years without learning something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. I'm learning a lot here, right now. Did you. . was it harder for a woman when you came to Portland, you went to school, you went into business on your own, was it harder in those days or was it easier for a woman?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wasn't difficult. I think a great dear of it was the attitude I had. I wasn't a dreamer but I could work out a thing and work toward it and was willing to put my shoulders to the wheel and work hard. And finally had my own [beauty] shop and four operators.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you keep the shop?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Long past retirement age, and then I worked a little while after that, but I worked for

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: others all my life, I've been a volunteer. I can't help it, I was brought up that way. On the farm you helped each other out. With illness, the farmer next door would even help with the crops. His wife went in a helped with the housework. That's the way we were brought up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of. . you say you still volunteer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I work as a volunteer at the Salvation Army, Senior Citizens, and I can't stand any more, I am a cancer victim. I can't stand, but I can sit and stuff that my hands can do whatever needs. Pulled a ligament here in my shoulder that's why I sit with my elbow on this and work with my hands.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Detennined to work.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you go stir crazy sitting in a place like this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: During the time you were at the Soap Creek, what do you think the most pleasant thing that you did for recreation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Riding a horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Riding a horse, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And none of this going around a ring or jumping a fence, in fact, when we sold some stock my husband got sick and my younger brother and I drove the stock down seven miles to the railroad and sold them all and I was thinldng the other day, wondering what we did about the saddles, then we had one horse to get home on and we did what the they call rides and tie. Do you know what that is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The fellow on the horse rides a mile and then he ties the horse to a fence post somewhere and starts walking and the other fellow walks up until he gets to the horse and he gets on the horse and he rides and ties. That's how my brother and I got home, we had one horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. [motions to turn off tape, then resumes]
bracketed_corrections: [motions to turn off tape, then resumes]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I want that clear that there was no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Animosity.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, and it wasn't any meanness or any. . not deliberate, just the nature. Lack of character.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm kind offeeling that. . one point I'm trying to get to; you ride horses and you did a lot work down in Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there wasn't much time for recreation.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Seems like you're still pretty nostalgic for that period, that that was a good period of your 4fè.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But really reading was my outlet. And at that time the State of Oregon had boxed books at the Library came from Salem and they sent them out into the rural areas and they were assigned to some farmer and then the whole neighborhood could borrow the books, a traveling library. And those books were always at our house, my dad, we had all the magazines that were going. Every child had a magazine come, you know, in his own name. You were taught to read and to think. And Mrs. Blake taught me a lot about reading. And if I couldn't read now, I'd be sunk. I tell you a person who reads is never alone though. You know, you'd be alone and there'd be times when you feel kind of lonesome but there's always the books.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: zat kind of reading do you do now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I like historical novels, and I like. . are you familiar with Dayton Hyde?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He's a rancher in Eastern Oregon, you've heard the story of "Sandy" the Sandhill Crane?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he's the one that writes those books, he's the one that raised little Sandy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: books. That type of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of reading did you do when you were a child?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you were at Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had kind of. . read every thing that came in the box. And there were chores to do when you got home from school, gather the eggs, feed the chickens, what else. . and always keep the hen house door closed. Took me out in the dark many a times when I had forgotten those. No danger, but scared kid you know. And then we had homework that had to be done, we had a gramophone and each child was allowed to pick two records and that was played and then we went to our school work. And then we could read, recreational reading. And many a time I slipped a book up under my skirt and took it up the stairs and read at night, well, mother got onto that on account that the light was still on. Kerosene lamps. I still do that, I stifi find myself reading when I could sit down and be perfectly comfortable and snitching time to read. Isn't that strange. I laugh at myself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I can relate.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I had a customer who was the same way, I think they were Quakers, and they said "Thee" and "Thou". The father and mother. But they let the children go to any church they wanted to. But anyway, this gal when she was married, moved to Spokane and her mother said. "now Edna, do Thy work first before thee sits down to read." And we laughed over that. And she told me, she was much older than I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One of your customers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Customer of mine. She told me a lot about the area around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm just now starting to study the Portland area, but this here depend upon building a potential.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Laurelhurst Park was a just a swale, she picked flowers, what they call spring beauties.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Soap Creek did you ever pick any of the wildflowers around there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. [yes - WMC]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you familiar with the dJerent varieties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not really, I mean, I couldn't give you the names of them, what we called the lamb tongues, a lot of them, that's what they call the Alpine Gold up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it's called lamb's tongue or Alpine Gold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And then there's the cat's ears, it's a furry little bell. It grows up here on the mountain. I've walked all over the Mount Hood Meadows, and I am very upset when I think of what they are going to do with it. Those hills were covered with phlox. I even found the real deer moss, a little patch of real deer moss, and I had it in a little dish on the desk and the gardener, a professional gardener came along and he saw that, and he came in the shop and said, "Do you know what this is?" and I said, "I don't know. It's moss and it looked good to me, and it's different." He said, "That is the real deer moss." And he said, "I'll bet I could tell you where you got it too," and he did. Now they're destroying all of that. The Mount Hood lilies, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that development. . is that what it is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What they're talking about developing the Mount Hood. . of course they've wrecked a lot of it already, now they're going to finish it. We used to walk all over that area, we went up about every two weeks and "side walk supervise" Timberline Lodge, young son and I. And they kept pushing and then they after they opened they had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds to me like, even though I'm only here because of Soap Creek Valley, a long but a real interesting and enjoyable life.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I love the outdoors.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have any regrets about anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to. . no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It doesn't sound like it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When they first opened up the [Columbia] Gorge, we used to go up there on the bus because we didn't have a car. Go up on the bus and then we'd climb the mountain and many, many a time hiked up Larch Mountain before they put a road up there. I resented that when they put that road in, isn't that terrible. But they didn't spoil things, it's beautiful and a lot people get to go up now that never could make the hike. Six and half miles up; every step of the way. Beautiful. Do it by moonlight and watch the sun rise.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right? That's. . my friend..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pick huckleberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. Too bad I didn't know you about seventy or eighly years ago. I go hiking in moonlight all the tune. My girlfriend think's I'm crazy, because she's never done that. I go and get my kids to go. Ican'tfind..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If my legs hadn't given out, I'd go with you. I'd go with you right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's my favorite time to hike and I've never talked to anybody that likes to hike at that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All the rustling things along the trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did very many people hike by moonlight at that time? I can 'tfind anybody.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. They did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Another thing that you said you didn't want to go into, but it's rather comical is the spotted owl. Didn't get recorded on that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know any thing about spotted owls. [Refuses to retell story]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you a member of any group like Mazamc or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. By the time that came along, I. . I've been to the top of Mount Hood. About sixty-five years ago, but no, I never joined, by that time I was alone and. . besides I didn't have time I had a living to earn. I did my share of taldng care of the kids and putting them through college.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You put both your kids through college?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Their father helped, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So both your sons are Oregon State graduates?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be great for the..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Roy will be interested, Dick wouldn't have known so much about it because he was born here in Portland. And when Dick graduated he was Second Lieutenant and went into the Service.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Does Roy have kids? I guess I can talk to him later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. He has four girls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The oldest daughter is the one that lives in Siletz.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's her name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sue. . Susan. . Sally's a teacher, she's married, she's not going to have any children, but she's a born teacher. And she's in California, now. She works very hard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Susan is she a Cook also?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they're all Cooks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Married name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. She's married now. Gudenow. Her husband is in the commercial fishing. But I think he'll probably give that up, it's not as lucrative, and then he's getting older too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing I'd like to do and I think probably today isn 't a good day, is to. . get this printed up and kind of tell where we're going and think as far as animals, 4festyle and how people lived and what was important to them, but then I'd like to on the next time, go through some spec jflc people that were your neighbors, like the Wiles, . . before we start the recording. And maybe this would kind of let your memory go a little bit back. . that was quite awhile ago. . seventy or eighty years ago.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Pause in tape. Mrs. Cook remembers a story she wants to tell and tape resumes after she starts.]
bracketed_corrections: [Pause in tape. Mrs. Cook remembers a story she wants to tell and tape resumes after she starts.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Woke up one night and I felt kind of queer, I wasn't afraid but I just felt as if someone or something in the room. And. . eventually I was started awake, somehow. . it wasn't a sound but it was kind of like. . swoosh . . right in the room and out the door. . the bedroom.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it scare you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Made you feel like somebody else there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I woke up I felt that there was someone there, but there wasn't anyone there. And I wasn't frightened, I didn't take it that seriously. Life's just a bowl of cherries you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you didn't hear the ghost stories.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it was years later that I told my mother about it. I said, "Mother, did I ever tell you about the experience I had when Roy was a baby?" My mother had been hearing a very good friend in. . when we lived in South Dakota that moved to Idaho and when our people. . my people moved to Oregon, they kept up correspondence and then she came down to visit two or three times on the farm, stayed a week or so. And when I told my mother, she said, "Now that's strange," she said, "Mrs". . I can't remember her name now (Tiffany), it'll come to me eventually . . but "Mrs. So and So slept in that same room and she said that she felt that the place was haunted."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Well, that's eighty years ago and then even now they're still talking about it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I was there. . it was about ten years ago since I drove up the valley and I took all afternoon; I had myself a ball just played along . . I have those often. . through all the dog gone Oregon deserts and Washington. . Walla Walla. . alone. . I loved it. When you're alone you can stop and stay as long as you want to. . in those days

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I could take a nap along side the road. . it was perfectly safe. Well, anyway. Mrs. So and So (Tiffany) said something about. but I didn't pay any attention to it. she said, that's strange, this is after we were here in Portland that I mentioned that. All right when I drove up there, I went. . asked them if I could see the house and I told them I said well, where's the fireplace? I thought maybe you'd have modernized the fireplace. Oh, is there a fireplace here. I showed them right where it should be. And they evidently just built around just when they remodeled. And they said something about the place being haunted. And these people are renting the house, I don't even know their names. But they were very nice to me and they said, "Come back anytime you want to." They were interested in what I could tell them, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's. . a lot of interest in thisproject was from local people there now are . . [camp] Adair came in and kind of stopped the history and now it's started. People are very curious about who used to live there and what they did and how they raised their crops.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At that time a building had been built where the spring house used to be, spring house is what we called it. And there were a couple horse. . fresh horses in the pasture, so I had to go over and pet the horses and so on. I really don't know if the spring is still there or not. It must be because they must. . they'd have to have a source of water somewhere, it was a beautifully cold spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you be willing maybe with your son sometime oh, later this fall or early in the spring to take a trip back to Soap Creek Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I would.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And we're standing facing some new construction on the southwest corner of the house, looking at some shingles. Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. Now, we're facing north, and on the west side . . . Well, there was a porch on this end, on the west end, and we used to have the wash basins out there and got the water out of the spring house, and the spring house set right in, right in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where this driveway is? Would that be.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right in there, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that little, u/i,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And we used to set all the milk cans and all that and then keep all the vegetables in the spring house. It was dug out and I think it was stoned up. I can't remember if it was concreted or not. That might be part of it, there, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This . . . but there used to be a spring right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That's probably where it was. It was directly west of the house. And there was a boardwalk, and right to the south was a wood deck in here and there was an old cream separator there, because I remember turning that god damned thing till I. making butter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of tree is this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Looks like an apple. I don't remember it. This is all grown up to beat hell. It was more or less open, like this. There were very. . . Oak trees were small and there were very few firs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come you 'd come here on the Marcks 'place? Didn't you grow up on the Cook place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I didn't grow up up there. I left there when I was five years old. But we'd come back, you see. And my grandmother still owned this place. My grandfather died. I never remembered him. He died before I was born.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember about your grandfather? Anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw him!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nobody ever talked about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very little. Her family were, I don't know, they were just not family oriented.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your grandmother. What do you remember about her?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, she was a hell of a good cook. And her maiden name was Maurer, M-A-U-R-E- R, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so, when you'd come here you'd be visiting your grandmother then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. For a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember. . . Do you know anything about those pine trees up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't recall. There were just a few trees. No, no pines that I recall at all. Just a few firs, and they were small. This has been pretty well logged off, or it was open anyhow, there was scrub oak and lotta grass, no blackberries like that at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody run any stock up in those zills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't recall. Vaguely, seems like it, but most of the stock was down below in the flats down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And do you remember any orchard or anything around in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn, no. Seerns like there was an orchard, but I don't recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You remember this house as being the house that was haunted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's the way I recall it. But that's all come out since we left, and my mother brought it up. All of a sudden she remembered and she told rne about it. As I recall, it was this house. It might have been the other one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I was hearing all these ghost stories down the road, and I wasn't paying any attention until I heard your mom saying it, then I thought well, wait, this is an old story.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there any. . . Now, yOu said the road coming in here didn't have the cut banks so it was all up and down.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, all up and down, just hurnpty-hump, there was no cuts in the road at all. It just followed the ground line. It wasn't contoured at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it was about the same basic location where it is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty much, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then, when it hit the house here, which way did it go?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It went on west for a ways, and then it swung down and rnade a turn down, there is a big house down in the flats down there. The road's changed now up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But we'll look at that when we get up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, on the back side, we've got the creamery, the spring house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was sornething on the other side, whether it was the creamery and so on, we'd take the milk cans out of here and churn that goddamned butter, and then there was something on the other side, and I can't rernember whether it was more like warehousy type stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, just storage or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Storage or sornething of that nature as I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I take it you don't like churning butter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't like washing the crank. 9 million parts...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This part of the house here, was it painted the same color?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was white. White or gray. It was light colored.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Looks like they're gonna keep it in shape.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Quite a rig in here. Quite a bit of hardwoods Looks like back east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Once they get a foundation on there she'll really be in good shape.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On this end here, did the driveway come in like this, or was this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it came in a little bit more down here. It wasn't level, it seems to rne we went uphill to go to the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, can we stop here for a second? Now, we're looking out. I think that might be Writsmans Hill, unless it's Writsman 's knob which is Baker Mountain. Do you recall anything about the.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] No, that's Carson Prairie right there. Baker and Writsman knob is further up.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that's what we 'ye got marked a.s Writsman 's Hill, because Writsman 's homestead went off that way. That's what we've got on maps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That's what we've got, but all the other maps show Baker and Writsman '5 knob further up... Being the same thing, though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] out there. Yeah, I know. On...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe that's it over there. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That's Forest Peak. Did you have any name for any of these peaks here? Do you remember what the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it seems to me they said that up in that gap up there, somewhere in that gap, there was a fortification5 or there was some old structures up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so that's on that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But I never went up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but that's on that gap right up through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was my understanding. And my memory is . . . I'd have no reason to retain it, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the prairie? Do you remember any

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It looks pretty much the same. A few more trees, over in here. It was more like Coffin Butte over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about. . . now, in this pasture here, were cattle being run, or sheep, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was cultivated a lot in there and there was a garden over in here, as I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any houses or old structures?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there were no structures that I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Okay, that Indian village by any chance wouldn't happen to have been.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was right down in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Okay, that's the same site. Down in this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right. Theoretically, just out there less than 1,000 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, your mom, she said.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, whether it was a village or not, but they were always picking up arrowheads every time they worked in the garden and so on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That's 35 BD 34. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Or 30. That's one of the Iwo registered sites on the forest when we came here. So. But your mom, when she was a little girl, had picked stuff?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, she had to work in the garden, you know, kids do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about these fences here? Were those those split railftnces? Do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think they were. They weren't metal posts, that's for damned sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Soap Creek there Now, you said you fished.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty much. Yeah I fished down there, but I fished more up above. Because I came, you know, I'd come back periodically. That was in, oh, 1920, 29, long in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many fish could you catch in a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All you wanted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Twenty or 30 or 50?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you never caught that many, because you just caught what you wanted for the house and that's it. You weren't fishing to be fishing, just digging around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what kind of trout they were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cutthroat, or something I guess. I don't know. I never paid much attention.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever do any hunting around in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I was too small.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear any stories about cougars or wolves or bears, or any kind of wildlife like that? Do you recall anything about the birds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Let's see. Can you think of any other questions at this site here Kevin?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] No, we need to follow up on the structures he was talking about up on Writsman 's

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was just, it's hearsay, but I can remember my dad talking about it. And I can remember my grandfather tailcing about it. Now, maybe it's because they went and ran fences down or something, I don't know. What the occasion was I don't know, but it was up, it was right on top, you see. I was a kid. I was curious. I wanted to go up there, and they'd never let me go, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it wooden or stone structures?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Log structures.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Whether it was a, just logs with no roof or what I don't know. But I sort of gathered it was just a barricade type deal similar to some of those in eastern Oregon, you know, a place where they can get behind or whatever. Now that's assumptive.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All these fields out here, those were your grand,nother 's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Now how far her property ran, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But it bordered onto the Glenders was the next...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Glenders then your grandmother's here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and how far it went down that way I don't know. But it wasn't a big place. I don't think it was, like the other places. Like the Cook place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could it have been 3(X) acres? Don't know, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything else around this one area here that you'd want to get recorded, or that you can remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, nothing.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B. Stage Stop Lane

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a fairly new school, you know what I mean.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is Stage Stop Lane, and this is the first time we've heard that there was a school up in this area here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a structure that looked like a school, it was right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. IKE V/NJ Just off the road there about 1 00 feet you think?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Yeah, ballpark.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe where that house is now? To the south of us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right about there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a structure over there by those large fir and that maple over there, on that little flat over in there to the right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't. I can't say there was or there wasn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: IKE V/NJ Okay, well here's a draw. Is this the draw that you were referring to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where the school . . .?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: IKE V/NJ Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm sure. Because it looks reasonably close to the same.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C. Browns' Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Close to those trees there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so we've just come down around the corner next to Goviers here, and you remember a house being out in here to the right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right in here somewhere. It was a pretty good sized house and it seems like there's another little lane went up to an old house in here. Now that may have been Govier's, but I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, right where those silver maple are there was a house that burned down [Hildebrand House Fire] in '37 or '38, that was the Brown place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That could have been the one. Yeah, it could have been there instead of there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about this house or anybody that lived in it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a great big two story house and painted yellow, and that's about the size of it. I can't remember names worth a toot. Names aren't my long suit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up here on the left we 're coming up to where the old Govier mill used to be. Do you remember anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. TJh, it sat over, right over here. It was a little gyppo mom and pop operation. It wasn't a big mill. It was right in here somewhere. Well, we're on a straight stretch, things have changed so much. Whether it was here or a quarter of a mile. seems like it was right in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D. South Boundary Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, next to the Govier's house, before you'd get there, there was a little road here, could it have been on that road on the left there? Okay, we're on South Boundaiy road, do you

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: know anything about. ..?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope, I don't recall a road there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or how about this side of the Govierfamily, do you recall anything about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was narrow. There were bushes along side of it. I remember you had to, you damned near rubbed into the bushes, particularly on up the line up there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E. Soap Creek Schoolhouse

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can we stop here next to the school house a little bit? Okay, there's an old tram road that used to go up to a mill right up on the turn here. Do you know anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about the school at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now there's another road turning down here to the right. There 's a German guy [Dorgan] that lived where that blue house is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] What about this structure.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember. It was probably there, but I. . . This road didn't exist to my knowledge. I don't remember it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Writsman 's Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't recall it. It could have been there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It may have been just a little road that went off to a little horse logging operation, you know. Used to be houses over there again, that's. . . And there were some Dorgans lived up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dorgans were in the blue house there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back there at the blue house. That was Dorgan 's, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that where they were?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were quite a family, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the only thing I can remember is that he worked helping with the logging and he took his lunch and she'd always wrap his sandwiches in toilet paper. It was sort of a standing joke. I guess she was, the hillbilly type. I guess she was a pretty good egg, though, from what my mom says.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was supposed to be a good musician. Did you ever hear anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't recall anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere over in there he. . . I think Mr. Dorgan got killed in a logging accident. Team of horses ran away, and they. . . He was dragging a log and he was standing on the log or something and the horses team. . . One horse went on each side and he baled into the trees, over in there 'cause mom used to point out where this guy got killed and it seemed like it was Dorgan I don't remember now. It was on the other side. He ran into a little grove of maple trees and he baled head first into a tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That would hurt.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [BREAK]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can remember the name. Somebody was always talking about "Junk."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Junk Matthews?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Junk, as if, just something about junk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Doesn't tie in, but I can remember them talking about the name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think your dad or youruncle found his body, according to the stories.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, maybe he's the guy that got tied up in the tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That'd be up here a little bit further.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: By gum, I think by golly that was right. I think it was Junk that got killed where they peeled into a tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That'd be right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Things are. . . don't look the same now. I'm sort of halfway lost now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here's an old orchard on our left here. And I asked.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're getting up here further than you used to be able to. Oh hell, it was down lower than.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Out there then, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I mean just below us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Oh, just below us.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F. The Cook Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It came up and had a real square corner here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, here 's the Cook place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Are these people anti-social?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, I think they're real social. But I've never met them. No, I met one of them at a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, I don't know whether I was born in this house or the other house. One of these two. Here, you want to get out?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right straight in. Down here a little further, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We came right in through there. And the house sat there, yeah. And there was a couple of little trees in there, and then that was pretty open in there. That hillside was all open.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Thai hillside to the west there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, those pictures that I gave you. Some of them are taken right up there on that hill looking down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the old orchard was around the corner there. Yeah, I used to have to take water and slop down to the damn pigs in the orchard there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That was a close orchard there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it seemed like it was a long way when you were pushing a wheelbarrow full of milk cans full of slop. And that barn sat on the other side of the creek down there. The road went down just about where that row of trees is down there, over a little

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: bridge, and then you came back this way about 400 or 500 feet and that was the barn and there was a garden right down on this side of the creek right down next to the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the Cook's garden? Somebody's garden.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it was Vincent's [Frank Vincent] then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. You talked about...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But that barn was in use. It was a pretty fair barn. As I remember I beat the hell out of a sheep over there. There was some guy by the name of Porter clear over by Kings Valley. He ran sheep and they had a "P" brand on the sheep, and they'd come over and they'd get through the fence. My job was running the damn sheep back and I got so sick and tired of it. They could find the hole to get into this property but they could never find the hole to get back out. So I grabbed a big piece of board off the side of the barn there and the sheep went past me and I nailed him right on the snoot and knocked him down. I thought I'd killed the damn thing and I was so damned little I couldn't carry him and throw him over the fence and I didn't know what to do and I didn't want to tell anybody so I just walked off and left him. Next day he was gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what. . now that hillside there. . . We got photos of that too. That was pretty bare, too, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty bare.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you run sheep up in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh, no, dad [Ernest Cook] didn't have many sheep. He had mostly perch [percherons] and horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When your mom and dad split up, did your dad stay here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they split up after they left this country. They split up about 1927.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what year they got married and moved here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They got married in 1914, I think. '14 or '15.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were born in 19--?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1916. So your dad had just finished up college then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And, was this house built new at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this house was already here when your...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's my understanding.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, for your edification, on that blacksmith's shop.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe I should go up and introduce us here before we talk too much fluffier.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All right.

entries.text: Was that shed there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. But that's where the barn sat. Seems like there was a little structure there along side of it. And God, I mowed hay in that damn barn until I was blue in

entries.speaker: A

entries.text: [KEVIN] Looks like an old . . [unintelligible] . right in through here. Yeah.

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, so the blacksmith's shop, the implement shop, the old barn.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It was more or less storage though. They put wagons and buggies and crap mit.

entries.text: [KEVIN] You don 'r recall this old . . [unintelligible]., back in there though?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There was a fence across here. And you had. . . If you go back in the woodshed you'll find a big bullet hole in the top of it where we shot a rat. We couldn't trap this sucker, we put a regular trap out he'd keep jumping over it. Wood rat. We unloaded on him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see now, these oak would have been here and these fir would have been smaller. Do you remember anything about the timber or the trees or anything through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very little. It was a little wooded, but nothing of any size. Not of merchantable size.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind ofa...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No pine trees. They weren't there. I don't recall any pine. And the dump for all the bottles and everything was on that side over there by the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, that would be interesting. So that where the creek comes down then there would be a bottle dump there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. Just right straight out from the house here. And then the old outer house I think it sat, no, it sat right over in there I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What are your memories of this house as a kid? Do you remember much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not much. The guy my dad leased it to, when he left in, I can't remember. There was a guy in between Vincent and my dad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Vincent lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember Vincent's first name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I was gonna say Frank, but I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But anyhow, there's, the guy, somewhere in the episode in there. He made moonshine in here and they raided the damn thing and he had his still and so on built in, alongside in the walls, along side the fireplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would have been -- Let's see, prohibition wos '18? '19?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was after that. It would be in the '20's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it in the '20's? Oh, that's right.

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just because he was making moonshine, huh?

entries.speaker: A

entries.text: What did he do after he left the fann here?

entries.text: He worked for Pacific Power and Light, only it was Northwestern Electric initially in 1922, or 1923 I think it was started up.

entries.text: I'm kinda cheating a little bit, because I've been back here with a little 90 year old man that could remember where everything was. There's a school gate there, we could probably turn around here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that cyclone fence is over there was an old [saw] mill from the 1890's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And maybe earlier.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What's inside that fence? Anything?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, school properly. This is about where the Cook place ended, right up in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it jogged around. The Springs wasn't on the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep. The Springs were owned by Bakers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Bakers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but now that you mention the name I remember hearing about the name. But there was just an old abandoned house, and it seems to me it sat on that side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About where that red house is there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It seems right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Did you ever go to Sulphur Springs for anything? To drink the water, or fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. No, I never fished up here, but I've fished in the damned stuff, and they should run it back through the horse again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Charlie Olson was there and he said the early families used to gather [the spring water] and they'd dñnk it for their health.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I've heard that too, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've talked to four people in their 90's with excellent memories, so it might be something to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My dad and mother [both lived well into their 90s} weren't too thrilled with it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's look at that Springs. I haven't seen it since year one. But I remember that it was sort of a mud hole sitting right in here somewhere, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we can go down there and check it out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's no water out here but there must have been . . . you can see the old alluvial plain out there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, there [untelligible] back there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this is up inside [unteffigible}. Wherever the canyons came down where there had been a water source where it narrowed down just before you get into the canyon, is always where you'd find the pulp wood. It got [unteffigible] everywhere down here. Mold. Black soil.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this was all .. . it was all open where the spring was. There was no brush.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, there's an old apple tree right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But the road came right close to the spring, it wasn't up there it was down in here somewhere. The road came through right along in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know anything about this apple tree here, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] See, this little crossing here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] This is it, right here. Do you remember that stone there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 think that might have been put in by the CCC's. Do you remember, does that spring look about the same as you remember it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what it looked like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a bank around. The bank was up about this high.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. About three foot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then the spring set down like that, and then there was little channel went off to the creek. But there was the high bank on three sides of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Was there any kind of a constniction or anything in the spring? it was just the pool like it is now but with the bank around it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have. . . do you remember any wooden stnicture or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, huh uh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] No cistern or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nothing. No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No walkway on the bank?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, huh uh. It was just, you'd walk out through the grass and there the damn thing was only it was down lower. How do they account for the presence of sulphur in here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, that's easy. With all the volcanic activily that took place in this area, all the basalts, and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, hell, that's true of Kings Valley or anywhere else. So why here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we get salt water over there [towards Arlie] and there's salt water on the other side of the hill [coast range], and salt water in Eddyville. Yeah, you go down a little bit.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll be damned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was locally recognized as a landmark pretty much, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At the other end of the valley would the landmark be Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah, Coffin Butte. I can remember. . . now that's one hill that I can remember a name on. But the others were just hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, but this was a well-known location and Coffin Butte would be a well-known location?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how about the valley itself? Was there anything within the valley that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Soap Creek Valley, is all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Well, let's see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And when they logged, they took the logs, when I was up here they took the logs to Suver and dumped them in the river and I guess they pulled them out in Salem or God knows where down the line.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they haul the logs down from here to Suver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Old beat up trucks. And I mean beat up!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long were the logs that they'd haul?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: God, I can remember bucking and. . . I don't know, 12, 14 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you buck with the misery whip or did you have chainsaws by then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hell, there wasn't any chainsaw! (laughs) Half the logs you pulled out you just drove the dogs in them, you know, and dragged them out with that and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Now, you've got this road identWed as a CCC or earlier? The trail that went out from there? I'd have to check my notes. I've got so much on this map that I can't keep some of it straight. This end of the valley is getting clearer and clearer as I talk to more people, but...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The creek seems smaller.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's. . . Charlie Olson says thesanie thing. Now, is this, that's not so soapy looking up in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not as much down below there. I don't know. But it still has that semi opaque.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever come up.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never fished up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you know jf there was any fish up in here? How about beavers, do you remember any beaver ponds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh uh. There could have been up here but I don't remember any down below where I fished. There's a lot of wind falls and so on, but no beaver dams or.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever go hunting at all for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not even for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was too young.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of a nice spot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In fact, my dad never went hunting, never went fishing, so I wasn't exposed to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ww would you go fishing with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Me?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: By myself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so there wasn't anybody.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I just cut a stick, for gosh sake. I didn't have a fishing pole.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [PAUSE IN TAPE]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: J. Lewisburg Saddle Viewpoint

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm gonna turn this on. Do you remember this field up here to the east of us? Is that north?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was open, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All these trees have pretty much come in then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Quite a view.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. There's Coffin Butte, and there's that new quarry we could see, and then that's the area, out through there, the Cook's place through there, and it came up in the draw through here. In fact I think the red house is right below the hill here. Can you . . . does anything out through here, do you remember any landmarks or does anything kind of ring any bells to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never saw it from this perspective.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was no houses out in through there, obviously. And we logged right along about where those little houses are down in there I think, because we weren't very far up the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you were on the toe of that hill there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, did that hill have any name to it that you can remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Baker's Mountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Writsman 's K'zob? Nothing like that. Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm a total failure on names.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that's fine. If you can't remember them, none of the rest of us even know, so, I mean, we can just put it down to your mom or somebody who an authority.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well things just didn't have names.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's so few fanjilies, youdidn 't need landmarks. Maybe the houses were the landmarks, you 'd just say "The Cook's Place," or the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, such and such a place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you remember the names of the places along the creek? Was it called "The Marcks' Place?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and the Cook place, and the Dorgan place, and the Glenders, and Goviers. But, and then you mentioned some names that, hell, I'd forgotten about, like Baker, I hadn't heard that, and "Junk" I hadn't heard that for, oh God, I didn't even know what his last name was. I'd undoubtedly heard it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Where did these [planted] trees come from? Urn, that was planted by Starker or somebody. That's the hill [Baker Mountain], Kevin, where the old line goes up to where Miller's house and Olsons were. And you don't rernernber the Olson's at all though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, for some reason or other it draws a blank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think they were before your time. They 're in their 90's, they 're your mom's age.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I draw a blank on that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, this is about the last stop I had here, is there, can you think. . . you 'ye got a few minutes left on the tape.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what it'd be.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [PAUSE IN TAPE - Tells a story]

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [LAUGHTER]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, when you were going to Oregon State, as a summer job, was that through the College that you ran those 3C kids? So that would be in the 30's, right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. 1936.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you do any work out at Camp Arboretwn?

entries.text: Okay, were there vely rnany College people from Oregon State that worked on Elliott State Forest at that time?

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Cook Family Photo, c. 1890. This photograph of the Cook family shows William Hunt Cook, his daughters, Doris, Lucine (called Lina), and Mary; sons John W. (left background) and Tyrone P. (on the right), and wife. Tyrone married the only child of Elizabeth Murphy and Judge Sylvester Schultz, but she died in 1899, leaving him with a son, Ernest, and a daughter, Mary. Judge Schultz died in Missouri in 1903 and his widow came to Oregon to be with her son. Wanda spoke fondly of "Aunt Bet's" visits to Soap Creek Valley and her stories of the Civil War (see page 22).

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following article appeared in the Rose Center for Seniors newsletter, probably in early 1990. Wanda often helped as a volunteer at the nursing home during her later years.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: How many of you who are reading this newsletter can boast of being born in an "itty-

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: bitty" town at the end of the railroad in South Dakota, or of climbing to the summit of Mt. Hood, or better yet of being almost 94 years young? I know of only one - WANDA COOK. Our Wanda has lived a very colorful life filled with fists and has created beauty and happiness wherever she went.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: By the time Wanda was nine, the family settled on a farm in the Corvallis area where

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: she spent the rest of her youth. Because S. Dakota had such sparse vegetation and Wanda had such a love for the land, she remembers with fondness the first blades of grass in the spring, the first violets, and of finding the Meadow Lark's nests in the tall grass. Her new home, Oregon, was always green. Another childhood memory - gathering grain under the grainery and chewing it for gum!

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Married at a young age, Wanda had two boys born in Corvallis but raised in

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Portland. When she and her young boys moved to the big city, many thing in her life changed. Wanda went to beauty school became a cosmetologist and soon owned her own business on 37th and Yamhill. Her shop reflected her love for nature, boasting of many lovely plants. Reminiscing just a bit, she recalled the time when it was safe to walk anywhere in the city. She and her boys took long walks, often to a mountain to watch the sunrise.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Loving the outdoors, there were many trips to the Mt. Hood area by bus, and the an

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: additional three mile walk to the Timberline area, watching Timberline being built, climbing Mt. Hood to the summit, finding dry moss and bringing it down (a NO_NO) - but it was worth it since is was real Deer Moss like found in Alaska. During those years, Wanda and her boys also enjoyed horseback riding, would rent horses on the mountain, and spend the day riding.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: An avid volunteer, volunteering before it was called volunteering, Wanda worked

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: very hard with organizations and on committees dedicated to bettering the circumstances in the local nursing homes.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Coming to Rose Center is therapy for Wanda. The center provides companionship

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: and lots of work caring for plants and working on the various projects.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: When asked what she would most want people to know about her, Wanda's reply

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: was, "My concern and interest in the fair treatment of the elderly in nursing homes."

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Regrets? That she didn't write down all of the grandmother stories she heard in her

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: beauty salon.

entries.text: [EVELYN] Uh huh. And then [pokes listener in the arm]. Twice, this time. And I said I'm not comfortable with this. I want you to go away. I don't want to. Because the book had told me, if you feel uncomfortable, they don't want to make you feel that way. So, she wanted me to read that book because she knew it would give me the knowledge to, then, when I got this paragraph that I was supposed to read from this minister, which really what it did it asked me and my guardian angel stood together and asked Jesus Christ to come and take this woman to her rightful place and told her that she was surrounded by God's light and was no longer bound to this earth. And in my mind I could see Christ coming down and taking her by the hand and they walked away.

entries.text: [EVELYN] No, I sat in the bedroom, upstairs, alone, by myself, and I could see this happening and my guide stood next to me. And when I opened my eyes I felt like I was in shock, you know, like all. . . I felt pale. And I said, boy this, you know, I really felt this. And my guide laughed and said, "well, No shit you did!" He talks the way I do you know!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [EVELYN] And he says just sit down for a few minutes. You'll be fine and then I was. And then we all noticed that definitely she was gone. And so then I was laying in my room one night and the fireplace was going and I felt comfortable and cozy and I realized that she had willed me here. That she knew that I was going to get this, that I had the know how. That I could get this piece of paper from my mother, and in my mind I said "Thank you for the gift of living in my house." "Well, thank you for the gift for the deceased.t' And I said "I wonder how long you knew that it would be me that would do this?" And she said, "well, you know, time is really different once you've gone on." And as she walked by me to leave she stroked my forehead, from here to here, and it brought me back to when I was 8 years old and I woke up in the middle of the night, I thought I heard my mother coming down the hail, and in walked this woman in a white flowing gown. And I, this person was coming towards me, and I was a child and I was afraid and I put the sheet over my head and I screamed three times and I felt my head be stroked from here to here. And that was her message to me. That "yes, this is how long I knew, and you were willed here."

entries.text: Endnote: 1. This facet of Evelyn's story has a curious corollary. Writing about a location a few miles north of her house in 1980, Jackson (1980:322-25, 382) wrote:

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Much of the recreation in the School of Forests in informal day use and as such, has not been systematically recorded. In recent years students enrolled in recreation management classes at Oregon State University have made periodic studies of recreation use patterns, but this information has not been made available. Common sights on weekends and during the week, particularly with favorable weather, are joggers, horse-nders, day hikers, bird-watchers, dog-walkers, photo-graphers, and other recreationists. Not as common, but unfortunately also present on occasions, are those who are illegally using the Forests for recreation. Some of these have been mentionedtrail bike enthusiasts, four-wheel drive vehicle operators, and illegal hunters. Rowley (1979) noted that some Ushady types of recreation occur:

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: a locked gate is a challenge to some people. UBy golly, I'm going to get in there and find out what's in there. U And when they get in there and find out that the challenge is getting through the gate, and I think another part is .... for drinking parties they get in there and know ... the sheriff or nobody else is going to catch them. They can throw a wild party, they can go park on lover's lane ... and they don't have to worry about anybody catching them. So there are the shady types of recreation illegal hunting. They know this is a refuge, and there's likely to be more deer there and easier to spotlight... (Rowley, 1979:13).

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Vernon McDaniel (1979) mentioned another Nshady recreation activity about which he heard many stories. About one-eighth of a mile from the sawmill that had been located on Calloway Creek, and near the present fence that demarcates the Nursery, a complex of several structures was erected. These served to house people who were associated with the sawmill. McDaniel was unclear about the date, but thought it was around the turn of the century. One of these dwellings operated for a time as a house of prostitution, according to the stories of long-time residents related to McDaniel. The house was located on part of the original tract purchased for the Arboretum by Peaby in 1925. McDaniel was told that the structure mysteriously burned, putting an end to the nefarious activities:

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: All the ladies used to come out from Albany, and Corvallis and around. So I guess the married women got tired of it and burned the house down.... They blamed the married women for it, but they kept their mouths shut. They didn't say anything (McDaniel, 1979:17).

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: McDaniel did not personally see any of the structures. Rowley has also heard similar stones about these activities at this location, and at several other sites in McDonald Forest. McDaniel remembered the location of another house of prostitution that was located on the fringe of the Forest. It was a short distance east of the Arboretum entrance (near Rt. 1, Box 327B); it probably operated during the 1890's. This one also burned after only a short time of serving local loggers, farmers, and other clientele, according to McDaniel. For several reasons, no first-hand informants could be found who could corroborate these claims U (Jackson, 1980:322-325).
